faq.q: Can we use Bible verses in a civil ceremony in Australia?
faq.a: Talk to your celebrant first. The Marriage Act sets the words that must be said, and personal vows, including verses, sit alongside them. Celebrants differ in what they are comfortable including, so ask early, share the full reading, and let your celebrant confirm the final wording and its place in the ceremony.

faq.q: Which Bible translation should we quote at our wedding?
faq.a: For printing and reading aloud, the World English Bible is public domain, according to its publisher. If you prefer the NIV, ESV, NRSV or King James Version, name it rather than printing its text, and ask your minister or celebrant which translation to read from; a minister may ask you to use the church's own.

faq.q: Why is 1 Corinthians 13 read at weddings?
faq.a: Our readings guide calls it the best known wedding reading, "often called the love chapter". Its verses describe love as patient and kind and say that love never fails. To use it inside your vows rather than as a reading, echo one line, such as "Love never fails."

faq.q: Can a parent or grandparent do a Bible reading at a destination wedding?
faq.a: Yes, and it is a meaningful role to offer. Send the passage weeks ahead, print it in a large font, and include the reader in the rehearsal. In a Catholic or other church ceremony, the priest or minister confirms who may read and which passages.

faq.q: Do we both need to quote scripture in our vows?
faq.a: No. One of you can open with a verse while the other speaks in plain words. Agree on tone and length beforehand, and tell your celebrant or minister so the two vows sit comfortably side by side. Respect for each other's faith matters more than matching.

faq.q: Can we print Bible verses in our order of service?
faq.a: Yes. The World English Bible's publisher allows copying, publishing and quoting, and asks only that a changed text not be called the World English Bible. Print the verse exactly, with its book, chapter and verse, and label the translation.
